Tech Report: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings.
  • Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics.
  • A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Sources indicate that traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can rapidly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

In a recent development, "The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," states Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information.

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating fresh ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster.

It has been revealed that working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

In a recent development, that process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

Recent findings suggest that "Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an notable step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," states Lei Du.

Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected swiftly and efficiently," notes Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers.

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," states Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control.

*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

It has been revealed that quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The viral story of a grandmother who accidentally invited a stranger to Thanksgiving dinner is being turned into a Lifetime movie, nearly 10 years after their unlikely friendship began.

Latest Update: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
  • Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy.
  • It has been revealed that in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

It has been revealed that in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

Recent findings suggest that "The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a upcoming generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," indicates DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

It has been revealed that mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

Using Light Inside Computer Chips.

Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

The compact DTU nanolaser is an notable step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers.

Recent findings suggest that the new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

Sources indicate that at its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use.

In a recent development, the next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

A chemical spill at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven saw the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) get involved, with between 5,000 and 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol confirmed to have spilled. The chemical is a heat transfer fluid used in a variety of products, such as antifreeze. The chemical ultimately found its way into a drainage ditch, but MDEQ has told residents that there is no immediate threat to their health or safety, according to local news reports.

Sources indicate that however, it has also been confirmed that water samples will be collected for further laboratory analysis while workers continue to clean the area and monitor for any further issues. It's also been reported that the chemical was contained to the drainage ditch and did not reach the nearby Horn Lake Creek.

In a recent development, it hasn't been a great November for SpaceXAI in Southaven. Earlier this month, it suffered a setback in a lawsuit over pollution in the area caused by its data center. The April 2026 suit targets the company's gas-powered power plant, which is used to supply power for its facility in the Greater Memphis area. It's argued that 27 gas turbines were installed without obtaining the required permits. It's also alleged that the plant could emit more than 5,000 tons of nitrogen oxides and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually. The company has tried to classify the turbines as mobile units to get around the glitch, but a judge rejected that manoeuvre.

Clearly aware of the local sentiment towards its presence, SpaceXAI offered a 50% Starlink discount to anyone living near its two Memphis data centers. It also remarked that it would waive the hardware cost, saving customers $349. SpaceXAI said that, between late June and early September, around 2,000 residents of the greater Memphis and Southaven area had signed up for Starlink connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that it was also recently confirmed that the City of Memphis was ready to make its first major investment as part of its newly introduced Community Benefits Ordinance, a fund that uses revenue from SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 facility. Almost $3.3 million will be pumped back into the city to help with housing and neighborhood improvements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hello! This idea started as a single theme week, which we thought we might run in the lead up to Grand Theft Auto 6's launch. Then it turned into a pair of theme weeks. Then we realised we had so much stuff - and that, frankly, GTA 6 would be so dominating it'll be around for far more than a week itself - that we couldn't really fit it into two weeks either.

So, allow me to introduce a whopping three-and-a-bit-ish weeks of specialist GTA- and not-GTA-themed coverage on Eurogamer! (Insert celebratory car horn toots here.).

With GTA 6 launching next Thursday, we'll start with a week of coverage dedicated to the series, beginning today with a reader competition (more on that shortly!) and running until next weekend. We'll be covering GTA from all angles here - retrospectives, features, launch day coverage and beyond - across the series as a whole, as well as the major one we've got coming up. You can see that in one place at our GTA Week hub, which will populate as stories go live.

It has been revealed that however! If that - coupled with the inevitable wave of coverage that already comes from an enormous moment in video games like this - sounds like the last thing you want from us, well frankly, we get it. Matching major games with big coverage is a part of the brief at a site like Eurogamer, but it's also far from the only thing we want to be about. And we know it's far from the only thing you're going to want to read about for the rest of November, either.

To counteract that, then: we're also running a solid two weeks of counterprogramming, beginning on Monday 23rd November after GTA 6's launch. Expect all things not-GTA: coverage of lesser-known games, smaller-budget efforts, in-depth features on games and stories that are thematically opposed to it, have nothing to do with it, or take it for inspiration but go in an entirely different direction. All of our special counterprogramming can be found at our Not-GTA hub here as it goes live.

Industry observers note that those of you who've been coming back to Eurogamer for a few years might remember our "Games That Got Away" theme week from a few years back - we're bringing that back in a modified form here, too. Look forward to dedicated write ups - some labelled as reviews, some as broader reflective essays and criticism - on some of the great games we haven't quite found the time for so far this year, as we look to clear our own pile of shame.

Amongst all this, rest assured that normal service is also continuing here as ever. All the essential reporting, criticism, guides and the rest - across all things video games, whether or not that includes the Big One - will carry on as usual.

Ultimately, our hope is to offer something for everyone with this period - both the people who look to us to be comprehensive across gaming's biggest moments, and those who see us as a place for deep, nuanced, or simply fun stories on the medium's lesser-known corners.

Thank you as ever for reading - we really do appreciate it. And on that note, here's a link to Bertie's blog on our readers' competition, where you can win yourself your very own copy of GTA 6.

#24114. Breaking: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that artificial intelligence is giving researchers a new way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit people.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that artificial intelligence is giving researchers a new way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

Recent findings suggest that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit people. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

Recent findings suggest that the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that reveals that the method is picking up a real signal," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them.".

What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials.

Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

According to recent reports, "Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns.".

Industry observers note that the distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

Recent findings suggest that "We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit users in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating.".

Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal.

The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet people to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

It has been revealed that "Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," notes Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report.".

Since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more quickly when millions of people begin using a drug.

"Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," notes Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight.".

AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible.

One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

According to recent reports, patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

According to recent reports, researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and swiftly.

"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," claims Sehgal.

Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts.

Sources indicate that the researchers stress that Reddit users do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

According to recent reports, even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

About 44% of customers included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.

More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

Nearly 4% of users who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

Consumers also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

Fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting.

In a recent development, one possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely important region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

Sources indicate that "These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," claims Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically.".

Industry observers note that the researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads.

For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," states Sehgal.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar indicates.

In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread promptly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among consumers may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move promptly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," indicates Guntuku.

It has been revealed that this study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

Netflix’s newest animated sensation, directed by Alyce Tzue (Soar) and John Ripa (Raya and the Last Dragon), dares to ask: what if Cinderella’s ugly stepsisters weren’t so ugly and bad after all, but were instead besieged by a Western world that reacted to their East Asian heritage with distrust and unease?

The answer is Steps, a film that turned out to be far more distinctive than the concept of fairy-tale revisionism it seemed to hint at. The relationships among Lilith (Ali Wong), Margot (Stephanie Hsu), the aforementioned ugly stepsisters, and Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) propel the movie from great to “must-see.”.

Industry observers note that its ending, however, might catch a few people off guard. Not because it’s particularly confusing, but because it takes the story of Lilith and Cinderella​​​​​​​ in a surprising direction.

The main plot of Steps centers on Lilith and Cinderella’s efforts to undo the harm​​​​​​​ their ex-friend, the bratty and insecure Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), inflicted on the kingdom of Alouette. All they need to do is get the glass slipper on Cinderella’s foot, and they’ll be transported to the night of the ball before Priscilla stole the fairy godmother’s (Bette Midler) magic wand.

Lilith and Cinderella manage to do so, but instead of returning to the night of the ball, Cinderella chooses to go further back—to the day she silently decided to shun Lilith and Margot in favor of Priscilla and the other Alouette residents who looked down on them.

In a recent development, by going back to that time and protecting her sisters, Cinderella changes everything. Lilith and Margot can embrace their East Asian heritage, and so can the people of Alouette. Fairy-tale creatures​​​​​​​ like trolls, previously seen as dangerous and unable to enter the kingdom, become accepted. There’s even a touching moment when we see​​​​​​​ two men dancing and holding one another on the dance floor, which, while not revolutionary, is still wonderful to see​​​​​​​ in a children’s movie.

At a press junket for Steps, Polygon asked the directors about the importance of that ending and what it meant to show a happier world where people embrace diversity and inclusion.

Recent findings suggest that “[Alouette] is a very small box of a kingdom in terms of its standards. So I love that, not only all of our characters, but the entire world changes from this one kind moment between Lilith and Cinderella,” Ripa explained.

In a recent development, before Lilith and Cinderella’s rekindling changed the kingdom for good, the people of Alouette were conformists; no one liked change​​​​​​​. However, in showing the acceptance of trolls and non-heteronormative pairings, Tzue and Ripa wanted to highlight the importance of everyone getting their happy ending.

It has been revealed that “We wanted to make sure that the idea of inclusion and belonging extends to everybody,” Ripa told Polygon. “It was one of the points of the film: everybody deserves to be a part of the fairytale.”.

Steps is now available to watch exclusively on Netflix​​​​​​​.

For more like this, see our GTA Week hub - or for the exact opposite, look out for our Not-GTA week of counterprogramming, running from 23rd November.

Industry observers note that UPDATE 17TH NOVEMBER: Firstly, a substantial thank you - THANK YOU - because your stories have been delightful to read. I've laughed and been touched by the power video games have to shape and compliment our lives, and to bring people together. You even inadvertently compelled me to send a message to the old friend I played Vice City and San Andreas with, to tell him what fond memories I have of it. "It was very intense," he replied.

Industry observers note that you had many similar tales, of friends playing together, siblings playing together, families playing together; heartwarming recollections of days when life seemed simpler. You also reminded me how games can fill holes in our lives and provide us with escapism when we need it most. And how many of you played the games underage! Some of you were scandalously young. But therein was planted a love for a series that remains to this day.

It has been revealed that the winning entry that I've chosen has continued to make me laugh since I read it. I enjoyed it so much I shared it with the rest of the Eurogamer team and my partner, who also laughed, which is a good sign. For me, this story not only gets at exactly what GTA is as a gaming experience, but also at the power games have to create bonds between people, and the quote the story culminates in is an all-timer: "I'm wanted for murder, Barry. Put the kettle on." Bradley Reiman, congratulations! I'll also pin the comment to make it easy to find.

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER:These are my favourite competitions to run on Eurogamer, so I'm glad to be able to announce a new one. We'd like you to share your favourite gaming memory related to playing a Grand Theft Auto game - any Grand Theft Auto game - in the comments below, and if we end up liking yours the most, we'll give you a copy of GTA 6.

Sources indicate that I love these competitions because they result in hundreds of funny, heartwarming and often poignant stories about playing games. We've done similar memory-offs for other major gaming franchises in the past: Street Fighter, The Legend of Zelda, Star Wars. We did one about Christmas. We even did one about Eurogamer for our 25th birthday. So it's only right that we do one for arguably the biggest franchise in video games: Grand Theft Auto.

I'll let this run over the weekend and put a deadline of Monday, 16th November at noon UK time on entries. I'll comb through replies early next week in the interest of selecting a winner and giving them - you? - a copy of the game before (or as) GTA 6 releases next Thursday. I notify people using the email address associated with their Eurogamer commenting account, and reply in the comments as well, making it explicitly clear if you've won. Please keep an eye on this thread and your inbox because if I don't hear back, I'll offer the prize elsewhere.

With that remarked, let's talk memories! I have a couple when it comes to Grand Theft Auto. My earliest memory is of a teenage me playing the first GTA at a friend's house. In a convoluted 90s way, one friend had taken their PC to another friend's house, where the three of us had assembled to play it. We'd take it in turns to burn around the top-down city, and when we weren't at the controls, we'd still be active in the experience, with the huge paper map unfolded, looking for spray shops the player could nip into when chased by the police. It was like being the passenger in a car. I can picture now, almost 30 years later, vividly.

The other distinct GTA memory I have is of playing Vice City and San Andreas one summer after I'd broken my arm and leg. I jumped off a roof in Australia when I was drunk; I wouldn't recommend it. Anyway, upon returning home, there wasn't a lot I could do - the breaks were both on one side so I'd crutch around (they gave me a wooden crutch in Australia) like a pirate - so a friend and I spent that summer taking turns playing GTA. It's all those shared moments laughing at Tommy Vercetti driving up staircases on vintage scooters that I remember, or CJ flapping his wooden-block hands around like paddles while gesticulating in cutscenes. Us just messing around. Friendship. That's what remembering Vice City and San Andreas conjures for me.

Industry observers note that but what about you - what do you remember about playing GTA games? Let your mind wander, let your mind remember, and thank you in advance for sharing your stories with us and everyone else. Have a lovely weekend.

Industry News: The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics.
  • Sources indicate that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics.
  • The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to latest ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

Sources indicate that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

Industry observers note that in 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," indicates lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

According to recent reports, when laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

Sources indicate that "We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

It has been revealed that when the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This indicated that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

"These results open a newly introduced direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

From Abstract Mathematics to Fresh Optical Physics.

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover upcoming ways to control and study light.

Nvidia notes it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials.
  • “There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right?
  • Recent findings suggest that instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd.".

“There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder mentioned. “But what we do have as a organization, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”.

Recent findings suggest that instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder states the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”.

Although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, shows up in two places. Grace, Finder notes, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.

Recent findings suggest that the picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.

This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”.

Industry observers note that although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”.

Sources indicate that as you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.

A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes quickly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.

In a recent development, finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder claims, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”.

This “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder said.

Vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already revealed that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the new Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

In a recent development, another week has climaxed and I'm so sorry you had to read that on a Saturday morning. But here we are again, with our regular feature, where we talk about what we've been playing in order that you do too. This week, Marie has been staring at monster butts; Connor has capitulated to World of Warcraft; Kelsey is discovering the joys of a beloved Zelda game for the first time; and Bertie enjoys someone being punched in the face, because I guess he's that sort of person?

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. And now onward!

Industry observers note that my favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone. Whether he means to or not, he serves sass all over town, and in Kakariko Village, and I am very much here for it.

It has been revealed that also, I wasn't prepared to come face-to-face with a monster's butt cheeks. At all. Imagine the scene: I'm enjoying the tunes of the Lost Woods, processing the changes that have happened to Hyrule in the last seven years, all while making my way to the Forest Temple. Then the Moblin's turn their backs to reveal... Well, everything.

This week I've spent an ungodly amount of time playing World of Warcraft: Forever (you may have read my preview on the website) and have been essentially glued to it during every minute of free time I've had away from work. I've got both my main professions above the level 225 mark and I'm firmly in the thick of it now. Levels take longer, items are actually getting good, and I've had to make a second alt character for extra bank space.

As a result, I've not been to the gym in a while. I actually got one of those emails asking why I've fallen off, offering some tips to get back into the routine. Sorry Nuffield Health, my sleep schedule is ruined and I've substituted proper workouts for squats and basic at-home cardio. Surely, this can't go wrong...

I don't have the same level of nostalgia for Ocarina of Time that my peers do, but that has not stopped me from enjoying every minute of running around Hyrule smashing pots and trying not to cry over the touching cutscenes and, well, Saria.

It has been revealed that the game feels like Dark Souls for children (endearing) and that is completely my jam. It's magical, satisfying, and often sad. There's creepy enemies as well as cute ones, trap floors and doors, mysterious NPCs... and my heart just feels so warm whenever I'm playing it. My fingers are now crossed that there's a Majora's Mask remake in the pipeline over at Nintendo. (As well as a Super Mario 64 remake, which I admit, is pushing it. But for what it’s worth, I'd probably sell my soul to see it get the Ocarina treatment.).

It takes me a while to settle with games; it takes me a while to settle full stop. I suppose in Fire Emblem's case I'm out of touch, seeing as the last instalment I played was on 3DS. But I struggled with the garish enthusiasm early on and the whole thing seemed overly simple. Nevertheless, I've settled a bit now, and now that the game's layering on more strategy and Intelligent System's expertise is coming to the fore, I'm beginning to enjoy myself much more.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn't expecting it to be quite so boobsy, though. Was Fire Emblem always this way? Perhaps it's my fault for picking the scantily clad queen Theodora, though that sort of presentation isn't reserved only for her. She's no wallflower, though. My favourite moment so far was when she got off her elephant during a parade - yes, her elephant - and walked over to punch a teenage boy in the face for halting proceedings. Apparently she was doing him a favour.

#24107. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1322 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
  • According to recent reports, until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
  • Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a upcoming approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

According to recent reports, until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a upcoming approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

It has been revealed that "We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," states Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Recent findings suggest that chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

The team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

Industry observers note that the physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

According to recent reports, "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Initiative Difficult Maneuvers.

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can blueprint difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

"If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How claims.

The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate swiftly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Sources indicate that experiments demonstrated that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up latest opportunities for multimodal locomotion," claims Hsiao.

According to recent reports, the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen states.

Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

Sources indicate that one major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also looks to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

bro what the hell is going on in the miencraft tiktok community 💔 pic.twitter.com/LRWY18yqx0.

#24105. Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future.
  • Sources indicate that legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power tech giant, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one.
  • This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for new transmission lines needed to power new data centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati, would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities.".

Sources indicate that legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power tech giant, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”.

This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for new transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies.

Sources indicate that this is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility organization in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away.

Despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.

#24104. Vice City was the GTA that established Rockstar's killer formula - and 24 years on, it's still one of the best games ever made

Vice City was the GTA that established Rockstar's killer formula - and 24 years on, it's still one of the best games ever made

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio.
  • Sources indicate that I can't verify the truth of this story.
  • And I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio. "I'm not going to work if this limey Brit is in here!" Houser refuses to leave, so the story goes - he just came down to meet one of his heroes! - and he and Reynolds end up chest-to-chest, about to come to blows, before a studio engineer breaks up the fight.

Sources indicate that I can't verify the truth of this story. It's one of those development rumours that's been around for a long time, originally written in a book about how games conquered pop culture called "All Your Base Are Belong to Us" by Harold Goldberg. But I like to believe it's true, because in this one moment, the two crucial strands of GTA: Vice City's DNA helix together: its star power and Rockstar's arrogance.

And I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all. I think a game of Vice City's scope - stretched to breaking with ambition, budget, and technical wizardry - couldn't exist without the ego trip of Rockstar at its highest. This is a game that (somehow!) started as a bit of DLC for GTA 3, supposedly intended to launch as a mission pack when Rockstar North figured out how to port it to PC. GTA 3 rolled out in October 2001, and by some miracle - and lots of crunch, no doubt - Vice City hit shelves in October 2002.

According to recent reports, this game - a game that would come to represent everything the GTA series is, for generations to come - was put together in about a year. I'd feel pretty full of myself, too, if I was able to crank out that sort of quality in that sort of timeframe. With a development budget of approximately $5 million (massive at the time, even though it seems paltry against GTA 6's rumoured $1 billion+) and a marketing spend of $13.2 million, Vice City's budget was indicative of a series shifting toward becoming a cultural milestone - a standard bearer for video games as a whole, and as explosive and attention-grabbing as Hollywood's biggest events.

Industry observers note that it's not like Rockstar needed to borrow credibility from the movie industry to inject some panache into its work, but even so, I think it's in its vortex of unbelievable Hollywood talent that Vice City really makes its mark. This was the first time Rockstar used a voiced protagonist, and by the developer's own admission, it was "a riddle" they had to solve. It didn't come easy; by making the protagonist a fullyfleshed-out character, players also had to like him - not an easy ask when he's a bonafide psychopath with a fetish for revenge like Tommy Vercetti. But Ray Liotta pulls it off without breaking a sweat. The actor has gone on record saying it was a rough gig ("You're creating a character that's not there before", he bizarrely complained in one interview), and Vice City director Navid Khonsari often moaned about the actor's unpredictable moods, so I imagine the mood in the booth wasn't great, but the result? The result is phenomenal.

You shouldn't like Vercetti. He's arrogant, he's brash, he's a totem for all the worst elements of misogynistic 80s excess. And yet, because he's such a cartoon caricature of a Miami gangster, he becomes a sort of quasi-romantic figure; a mob stooge who's been set up by his old 'business associates' and by the very fabric of the American Dream. Vice City is, in a sense, a redemption story dressed in the clothes of a revenge one. Vercetti dreams of being a self-made man, of taming this latest frontier of unbridled capitalism and clawing back the years that were taken from him by the mob in Liberty City.

From the moment he arrives in town and a cocaine deal swiftly goes south, Vercetti is on the back foot. In the opening hours of the game, he - and, of course, you by extension - work for pocket change, picking up menial jobs here and there while meeting all the freaks and strangers Vice City has to offer. There are no less than 50 story characters here, brought to life by Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, Danny Dyer, Philip Michael Thomas, William Fichtner, and many, many more besides.

Playing Vice City again in 2026, I was absolutely floored by this cast - and how well their personalities and mannerisms translate to the almost puppet-like visuals Rockstar deployed for the game. Reynolds - despite not having a good time in the booth, if the story up top is anything to go by - is a highlight; the bombast and bravado of his Avery Carrington feels like a prototype for some of the more extreme characters we meet later in the series. I think I can even see a bit of Trevor in him, you know? It's how the Housers would take a trope - say, ruthless Texan oil magnate - and amplify it to its furthest, most cartoon extreme: what does this person look like with all the guardrails off, with the heady intoxication of unlimited capital at their disposal? For Trevor, that trope is 'unhinged redneck' and the cartoonish extreme is 'without a single shred of a conscience'. You can apply the formula to just about anything in the series, and it makes sense.

For Tommy Vercetti, though, it's slightly more nuanced. He isn't just 'Scarface' with a touch more humanity - no, he's a tragic figure, betrayed by all his closest friends. In striving to take back some power and gain a little more control over his life, he ends up decapitating the local drug smuggling scene and taking over as its head. The first half of Vice City is Sisyphean; an endless, uphill slog to scrabble just enough money to get by. Then, all of a sudden, the world opens up: you're now head of a drug smuggling ring, operating out of a suspiciously Scarface-like mansion, with the city at your fingertips.

In a recent development, the way the game, previously tightly-coiled and a bit miserly with its freedom, now unfurls in front of you is a perfect reflection of this upcoming-found power. Suddenly, your world isn't governed by the little mission icons on your minimap, you're not being told what to do over the phone by contacts wanting something from you. No, you're calling the shots. This is the 80s, so those that are making it significant are making it big, and those that are failing are failing. In a breathless display of uber-capitalist Yuppie thinking, you can even buy out nearly-bankrupt businesses and run them to your liking. The strategy is two-fold: one, you gain fronts for your other illicit activities, and two, you diversify your income streams and safeguard your assets should any one element fail.

And it's here, in its glorious second half, that Vice City becomes a breezy, beautiful bit of open-world catnip that fuses gameplay and story in a way few games have done so successfully since. You can buy a strip club (where you can launder cash), the Malibu Club (which comes with an outlandish set of missions culminating in a heist), the Cherry Popper ice cream van tech giant (a front for dealing), the boatyard (a drug smuggling base run by two excellent potheads), Sunshine Autos (a fence for stolen cars), Kaufman Cabs (headed up by an old controller played by Debbie Harry), Interglobal Studios (an adult movie production company), and the Print Works (a counterfeiting operation). The roleplaying as Vercetti takes off; you're a bigshot touring his empire, helping out here and there, meeting your crew, setting up deals. This should feel like drudgery; workaday tedium unbecoming for a legitimate businessman like yourself. But every job, every bit of flavour text and dialogue, feeds into your growing sense of power… and Vercetti's unstoppable ego.

In a recent development, alongside these key story beats are Vice City's non-essential tasks - which feel like a precursor to the 'Strangers and Freaks' missions in later GTA and Red Dead games - including the Love Fist missions. These, I think, are the best missions in the game (I'd also like to note here that 'Jez Torrent' is an amazing name for a New Wave of British Heavy metal frontman). But it's the way these core and non-essential missions dovetail that feels so great, and where the open world of Vice City really comes into its own.

In many ways, Rockstar's work here created the blueprint for what would become the Grand Theft Auto 'formula'; galvanising cinematic setpieces with free-roam activities and meta-progression that manage to alloy player agency with this sense of perpetual, unstoppable momentum. And it's all fun, too. There are some abysmal tasks, sure - piloting RC aircraft to ruin building sites, navigating boats with the wonkiest physics you've ever seen around stunt courses, waiting 15 minutes a pop for rare cars to spawn - but generally speaking, Vice City has the fun factor.

In a recent development, I don't think that's something I can say of other GTA games: I think often, they're a bit bloated around the middle, padded out with baggy missions and feckless busywork to give the illusion of depth and breadth. GTA 4 is also one of the most dour and oppressive open worlds I've experienced (this is a compliment, mostly), but it's not particularly fun. GTA 5, especially the Trevor segments out in the rural counties, can get a bit one-note - why introduce us to this massive world, to the state of Los Santos, if you're going to quarantine us to the rural outskirts when we're just starting to familiarise ourselves with the city? Why put up rails in a world begging us to revel in its open-ended sandbox? The only time that happens in Vice City is at the start, and the game is better for it: 'if you want to live the Scarface fantasy, buddy, you've got to earn it'.

And there's so much to love about the vibes of Vice City. The guys in shorts smoking pot on the beach; the girls in bikinis rollerblading down the promenade; the neon-drenched slick of a Florida night in the rain; the still-unbelievable who's who of music, deployed with panache in certain cutscenes; the incidental chatter of coked-up presenters on the radio; the distinct realisation of the Haitian and Cuban districts on the map; how 'downtown' actually feels like downtown. You'd think all this would have aged out of relevance by now - especially with GTA 5 being as lush and premium as it is - so it's a real credit to all those Rockstar employees that no doubt spent countless nights sleeping under their desks that Vice City still feels this good now, in 2026.

GTA: Vice City is still one of the best games ever made, I think, and probably one of the most key, too. Buoyed by Rockstar's ambition, and propelled to mainstream success by the strength of its cast, it represented video games coming out of their awkward teenage years and blossoming into young adults; biting off slightly more than they could chew, but cocksure and confident all at the same time.

Given how much of Vice City is built around the visibility and power of its cast, it's disappointing we're never going to see these characters really represented in any other GTA title again. Liotta, already unhappy about the process of recording his lines, reportedly refused to come back as Vercetti for San Andreas. And that's a real shame because - by former lead writer Dan Houser's own admission - Liotta saved his "awful writing" with his talent. The actor passed away in May 2022.

In a recent development, though he balked with Reynolds, Vice City director Khonsari could usually corral the rampant ego of his Hollywood hires in the GTA studio. "If you want me to break it down to you," he’d say, "these games gross over half a billion dollars, more than all of your movies put together!" I think you can see that bravado in the spirit of Vice City, and reflected in the runaway ego of Tommy Vercetti. And I think - without that almost toxic sense of self-belief - Vice City would never have happened.
