📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a latest generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an notable role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides newly introduced insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

In a recent development, rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an key advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," noted Sudbø.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Newly introduced Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly vital if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

Sources indicate that the findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

Sources indicate that "The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become vital for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Breaking: The Nvidia CEO scandal is impacting Asian American women in tech and academia. Here’s how

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent.
  • The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent.
  • Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy.Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women,” mentioned Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people’s opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It’s a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy.“I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” President Donald Trump told reporters this week. Asian women struggle to be taken seriously as leaders Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”Depicting them like trophy wives “implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions.“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, said Rachel Lee, the organization’s president and general counsel.“It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said.On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were ‘I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership,” said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network. Stereotypes around Asian women go back centuries Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the U.S. under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy,” Chai said. “It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added.The headlines had Chien reflecting on when she played a spy in a building security ad in Hong Kong 20 years ago. She was instructed to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie’s figure. She wrote an Instagram post to point out “how the media enjoys putting Asian women in that kind of role” and urged women to not let people’s assumptions keep them from success.“So many followers messaged me saying ‘thank you so much for speaking up,'” Chien said. Real harm can come from stereotypes Suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. Over two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in American universities has fallen. And the first Trump administration created a initiative known as the ” China Initiative ” to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors.Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the U.S. for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything.“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.“Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the U.S. president.”Ideally, Lee said more companies should allow for education and training around the harm and history of stereotypes. She encourages any woman who has had uncomfortable interactions to reach out to advocacy groups such as Stand with Asian Americans if she has nobody to turn to at work. At Stand with Asian Americans, people do not need to have a legal case of discrimination or harassment to receive assistance including education on their rights and mental health support.Individuals also have the right to draw boundaries and make clear what’s not OK to say, Lee added. It’s in employers’ best interest to make sure no federal laws against discrimination and harassment are being violated.“It’s a win-win to have that conversation,” Lee said. —Terry Tang, Associated Press.

#24068. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2311 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

Sources indicate that this unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

In a recent development, "In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

Sources indicate that to minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

According to recent reports, although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

It has been revealed that superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the fresh approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

Recent findings suggest that "It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

It has been revealed that the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

Industry observers note that according to the latest research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

It has been revealed that this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Industry observers note that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

According to recent reports, "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," states Egues.

It has been revealed that this behavior is notable because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

Recent findings suggest that in quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

In a recent development, these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

Sources indicate that the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

Sources indicate that "All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

It has been revealed that from a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising newly introduced way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability.
  • You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.
  • Industry observers note that the actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability. The researchers say it rates 9.2 on the newer CVSS 4.0 scale, though individual reports from companies like Oracle itself and Red Hat give it their own ratings, but they're all in the 8 to 9.8 range depending on the vendor. The root cause is a bug in OpenJDK, the library that nearly every distribution of Java, whether Oracle's or anyone else's, derives their implementations from.

You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.

Industry observers note that the actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language. Base64 is a format to allow for easy transformation of binary data into plain text. In the modern day, it's used to embed files in the middle of text, like inserting image data in the middle of HTML or CSS, attaching files to emails (internally they're all text-based), or simply representing data as text for visual inspection, like file checksums or cryptographic key fingerprints.

Industry observers note that oracle has already fixed the bug and issued updated versions of its wares. However, much like digital certificates, operating systems and even individual programs include their own copy of a Java executable, meaning that the potential blast radius is far wider than you'd expect at first glance. Calif listed many such common applications: at the time of the post, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and PingFederate all had full unauthenticated RCE, while Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker have RCEs after authentication.

Because Java is so darn widespread, most every organization has to concern security advisories and updates for their wares, including IBM, Red Hat, Siemens, and Broadcom. Because so many containers also use Java-based applications in some form, those too are vulnerable, and the count of individual vulnerable container images across registries everywhere is likely a high figure. This is likely not a bug that will be easily eradicated.

Sources indicate that there is a condition to trigger the exploit, but it's not too difficult to fulfill. The Java instance in question must be running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 support and the VBMI extension. In practice, that means chips from the Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 4 families, from 2021 and 2022 respectively, for their server variants. Older CPUs are not affected, as the code optimization that contains the bug is specific to VBMI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The specific bug is in a hand-written assembly optimization that fails a simple bounds check. If an attacker inputs 64 As and an "=" sign as padding, they can overwrite neighboring memory, and then weaponize that corruption, similar to how Heartbleed worked. As usual these days, Calif states that the vulnerability was found by an AI bot, with $200 worth of tokens. Though unlike many other examples, this one was actually fairly deep, and it wasn't low-hanging fruit that illustrated poor code or network security hygiene.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s not just tech and AI stocks getting hammered lately. Gold investors are also seeing significant losses. As of this writing, the precious metal is down nearly 3% for the day, trading just above $3,576 per ounce. That’s a level the yellow bullion has not seen since September 2025. That price is all the more striking when contrasted with gold’s surging value earlier this year. In January, gold peaked at around $5,600. But since then, the precious metal has been under constant pressure, and in late September, its price began plummeting from around $4,400 an ounce to roughly $800 less today. But just what is driving gold’s fall as of late? There seem to be three major factors impacting the bullion’s recent plunge. Expected Fed interest rate hikes The first factor likely influencing gold’s fall recently is the likelihood of a federal interest rate hike in December. As Fast Organization previously reported, the Fed is likely to raise rates by 25 basis points, to a range of 4.00%–4.25%. When interest rates rise, money becomes more expensive to borrow. This means the lenders of that money stand to make more. Anyone can become a “lender” by buying Treasury bills whose interest rates are heavily tied to the Fed’s set rates. Rising interest rates typically lead investors to sell off non-interest-yielding assets and use the proceeds to buy assets—like Treasury bills—that return a guaranteed rate. This asset reallocation is likely one of the major factors affecting gold prices (and not just gold—but also cryptocurrency prices lately). The tech and AI sell-off The second likely major factor impacting gold prices lately actually has nothing to do with gold itself. Rather, the rut in tech and AI stocks can be to blame. Since October, tech and AI stocks have been under sustained pressure as investors have grown increasingly concerned about what many see as out-of-control, unsustainable capital expenditure by AI hyperscalers. Critics argue that this massive capex spending—to the tune of hundreds of billions—can’t last unless the hyperscalers can start generating sizable returns, something they have so far been unable to do. Investors worry that if revenue (and profits) can’t materialize, the hyperscalers will cut back capex, sending the business of AI component makers like Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Micron, and more into a downward spiral. As these concerns take hold, investors are moving out of high-volatility tech and AI stocks, taking profits and sending shares lower. But not everyone is taking profits. Some investors are cutting their losses, and when they do, they also tend to sell other liquid assets, like gold, to cover them. A stronger U.S. dollar Finally, another problem for gold is the increasing strength of the U.S. dollar. Since September, the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) has increased by more than 4%. The DXY tracks the U.S. dollar’s value relative to six foreign currencies: the Euro, Yen, Pound, Swedish Krona, Swiss Franc, and Canadian Dollar. A strengthening dollar can be a problem for gold because the bullion is priced in U.S. dollars. When U.S. dollars become more valuable relative to foreign currencies, international demand for gold usually slips because it costs foreign investors more to buy the precious metal.

When the client is a good fit on paper, but still not a good fit

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was so excited to work with a new client.
  • A perfect match for my expertise, and the type of organization I prefer collaborating with.
  • It has been revealed that but once the contract was signed, it was a struggle from day one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was so excited to work with a new client. A perfect match for my expertise, and the type of firm I prefer collaborating with. Meeting the client for an exploratory call felt like a dream. A well-respected brand to add to my portfolio. But once the contract was signed, it was a struggle from day one. We parted ways six months later. Most advice about struggling client relationships assumes there is an obvious problem, like that the client is overly demanding or hard to reach. But in this case, it was something else. The vibes were off. When that happens, it’s less obvious what to fix. Recognizing the difference between a difficult client and a poor fit can help you decide sooner whether to adjust the working relationship or simply walk away. Why a client can look right on paper and still not work The things I vet for during the sales process can be different from the things that make a working relationship successful. Before signing, I look at the potential client’s industry and the scope of work. The client’s budget has to be aligned with my rate, and I have to feel confident that I can deliver what the client is asking for. That’s the relationship “on paper.” But what’s often unknown is how the client interacts with a consultant or contractor (like me). I’m also unaware of any internal politics at the company that might impact the working relationship. Those details usually become apparent once I start delivering actual work. Is it a difficult client or a poor fit? A difficult client has problems like not paying on time or asking for work outside of the scope. These can be fixed (or at least managed) with a solid contract and clear boundaries. Most of the biggest client red flags that solopreneurs face are in this category. A poor fit is different. The client may pay on time and stay within scope, but other parts of the working relationship feel strained. Maybe stakeholder feedback gets under your skin because of how it’s presented. Or you find yourself dreading the work, even though, on paper, it’s what you had agreed to do. One thing to ask yourself: Would a different consultant or contractor have the same trouble with this client? If the answer is yes, you’re likely dealing with a difficult client. But if you can picture someone else doing great work for them, the problem is probably the fit. A second question: If this client always pays on time and never asks for anything outside of scope, would you still want the work? A “no” usually means that fit is the problem. What to try before you walk away A poor fit sometimes might improve if you’re able to directly address the thing that’s causing you angst. It’s worth trying before you decide. If the problem is, for example, “too many cooks” providing you with feedback and contradictory opinions, you might be able to solve this. Something like: “It’s easier for me to make sure I deliver what you need if you consolidate your feedback. Can you work on your end to send me a list of thoughts/changes? That way, I don’t start down one path only to find that you want me to go in a different direction.” In some cases, your client might be willing to change—they may simply not have experience working with a contractor or consultant. You might also give yourself a checkpoint, like an additional month of work after the conversation. If nothing has changed by then, you have your answer. Admitting the relationship isn’t working When you work solo, a poor fit can drag you down. In a company, a colleague might take over the account, or a manager could reassign the work. As a solopreneur, there’s no one to hand it to. And since your income depends on the work, ending the relationship means replacing that revenue. But staying has a cost. Stress. Frustration. All the things you were supposed to escape by choosing a solopreneur life instead of a corporate job. If the conversation with your client doesn’t change anything, more effort probably won’t fix it. At that point, calling it a poor fit and moving on is a business decision. It helps to remember that a poor fit says nothing about your skills or the client’s character. It simply didn’t work out.

#24062. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • Recent findings suggest that but position and time are different.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

Recent findings suggest that but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

It has been revealed that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

Recent findings suggest that at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

It has been revealed that tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with key changes taking place over just attoseconds.

In a recent development, to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

Industry observers note that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a fresh laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

It has been revealed that the researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It demonstrated that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

It has been revealed that to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

According to recent reports, for example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

It has been revealed that raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

Sources indicate that in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists newly introduced ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

It has been revealed that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

Industry observers note that "In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the presently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a newly introduced foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#24060. Silicon Valley’s reaction to the Nvidia drama is rife with blind spots

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3566 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Silicon Valley’s reaction to the Nvidia drama is rife with blind spots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company’s Plugged In.
  • Hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company’s Plugged In.
  • Jensen Huang was scheduled to speak at this week’s Semafor Silicon Valley & The World conference, which he cochaired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company’s Plugged In. Jensen Huang was scheduled to speak at this week’s Semafor Silicon Valley & The World conference, which he cochaired. For reasons too obvious to require explanation, he didn’t make it to the event. And yet he dominated the on- and off-stage conversation so resoundingly that it might as well have been titled “Silicon Valley, The World & Jensen Huang.” As tech notables sat for interviews—among them Sam Altman, Clay Bavor, Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy, Yann LeCun, Fei-Fei Li, and David Sacks—moderators kept requesting their take on Huang’s shocking ouster from Nvidia. Most lavished praise on his entrepreneurship, but begged off saying much more on the grounds that the circumstances remained murky. Bezos’s comments were typical: “I don’t know enough of the details and I think probably most of us don’t know. . . . What I can tell you for sure is that Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company.” Jeff Bezos speaking at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World on November 17, 2026, where he called Nvidia’s Jensen Huang “a remarkable guy.” [Photo: Kim White/Getty Images for Semafor] Speakers at Semafor’s event approached the subject more gingerly than many in the scrum on X where Huang declared on Tuesday that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Skimming the 58,000 replies to his post, I didn’t see much discussion of the specifics of the case: Huang’s confessing to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia business partner who was allegedly also a spy for China, the questions that raised relating to Nvidia chips possibly being smuggled into China, and reports that he had two additional affairs with Nvidia employees. Instead, Huang’s X followers mostly had his back. Tech industry celebs such as Aaron Levie, CEO of Box; Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril; and Linda Yaccarino, former CEO of X, shared a few words (or emojis) of support. Others were civilians who expressed their enthusiasm for Huang’s theoretical rehiring in the form of truly weird AI slop: Jensen as Jesus at the Last Supper, Jensen popping out of a casket, Jensen lip-syncing Michael Jordan’s comments upon his return to the Chicago Bulls. Despite reports of disagreement among Nvidia’s board members, the company continues to rule out Huang’s return. Given the unfolding legal and geopolitical elements of the story, a speedy Sam Altman-style reinstatement would appear to be fantasy in even the rosiest of scenarios. The revelations thus far have already prompted the Trump administration to tighten restrictions on chip exports to China. Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 1. Democrats, who will regain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in January, are salivating at the opportunity to dig into questions such as whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick facilitated the diversion of Nvidia chips to China. And California’s attorney general has subpoenaed Nvidia in search of any evidence that Huang’s affair led to chips or confidential information making their way to China. Bottom line: Everyone who notes we don’t know enough to come to a firm conclusion about the precise nature of what happened and its appropriate repercussions is on far firmer ground than those who think Huang was unfairly forced out and should be welcomed back. But for all the miasma of uncertainty clouding this drama, it’s already told us plenty about Silicon Valley. Its most admired, envied, seemingly essential CEO being shown the door, even as the company he cofounded is still booming, is a deeply unsettling black swan event, and I haven’t seen many in the industry unblinkingly confront its implications. It’s surely not a coincidence that Gina Raimondo, the former U.S. commerce secretary—who is a technocrat, but not a creature of the Valley—had the bluntest assessment of the situation I heard at the Semafor conference: “Any kind of corruption, politics, dealing with spies, [there should be] no tolerance for it.” Paul Graham, cofounder of Y Combinator, coined the term “founder mode” in 2024. It celebrates startup founders who refuse to cede control to professional managers, regardless of how massive their brainchildren become. Decades before the concept had a name, Huang exemplified it. Instead of growing more remote from the minutiae of the company’s operations as it became a behemoth, he had his hands in everything—which is how he wound up with a reported 60 executives answering directly to him. Over Huang’s 33 years as Nvidia’s CEO, he took risks that no MBA-brandishing suit would have dared. None was gutsier than his 2006 decision to pivot from focusing on 3D graphics to building a high-performance general-purpose computing platform. That prescience paid off when artificial intelligence became an epoch-shifting opportunity, leading to the company’s 90% market share in the chips that power generative AI. In recent years, as Nvidia has jockeyed for the title of the world’s most valuable company, Huang has been no less daring. Whatever you think of the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which many players take financial stakes in their own customers, Nvidia’s willingness to write huge checks to companies in its own ecosystem has been critical to AI’s growth. And as expectations for the technology prop up the stock market, it’s not just the tech business that might look very different without Huang’s high-stakes gambling. So might the entire U.S. economy. Huang the public figure has become as unique as Huang the fearless entrepreneur. Once an unassuming engineer in an Nvidia shirt who went by his birth name of Jen-Hsun Huang, he reinvented himself into the genially bombastic, leather jacket-wearing rock star I interviewed in 2024. Only Altman rivaled his omnipresence as a speaker at tech industry events. Huang, who relished engaging in stunts such as frolicking with robots onstage, was a lot more fun. I can understand why people who never met him take his downfall personally. If you can’t envision a tech industry without Huang at its core, you have every incentive to wish for any possible outcome that would reinstate him to his previous eminence. But Huang himself took risks that made a happy ending far less likely. All evidence indicates that his initial strategy for dealing with the mess he created involved misleading Nvidia’s management and board, not to mention members of the press. Huang’s undisclosed relationships seem to have violated Nvidia’s own code of conduct. I have seen many people argue that they should still be forgiven. But to my knowledge, nobody has explicitly maintained that a CEO lying to his board is tolerable, at least if that CEO is Jensen Huang. Maybe that’s because the case is impossible to make. Another bad bet Huang made was his tight relationship with President Trump, which he was flaunting as recently as September. It apparently influenced the president to dismiss an October 2025 intelligence briefing on Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice (no relation) Huang. Trump may not have been doing Huang any favors, given that the story blew up in both of their faces at the worst conceivable time, after the Democrats’ wins in the midterm elections. As Daring Fireball’s John Gruber noted this week, tech executives have historically steered clear of hugging any political party so close that it would complicate their relationships in Washington, D.C., should the balance of power shift. Huang abandoned this approach during Trump’s second term. So did other executives, but only Elon Musk may suffer graver consequences. Huang’s unplanned departure also left Nvidia scrambling to deal with a fundamental bug in the logic of founder’s mode. Any company that’s lucky enough to matter for decades will, at some point, be run by a nonfounder—maybe even a dreaded professional manager. Responsible founders, no matter how hands on, should prepare for that day. Many do not. Along with everyone else in the Valley, Huang apparently couldn’t picture a post-Jensen Nvidia. I hope he was kidding when he said he’d like to run the company for another 30 or 40 years and then be replaced by a robotic version of himself. But his failure to establish any clarity around a succession plan is a deadly serious problem for the company he founded. (His daughter, son, and son-in-law all work at the company, but not in roles that leave any of them as an heir apparent.) Nobody else in tech ever had a career like Jensen Huang. His present quandary is part of that story, but I don’t expect it to be his only legacy. He might even rebound in some manner that doesn’t involve him getting his old gig back. Assuming the mystery surrounding this chapter eventually subsides, I hope the facts of the matter leave the industry wiser—if sadder—about aspects of its culture that it usually does its best to ignore. As tech notables sat for interviews—among them Sam Altman, Clay Bavor, Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy, Yann LeCun, Fei-Fei Li, and David Sacks—moderators kept requesting their take on Huang’s shocking ouster from Nvidia. Bezos’s comments were typical: “I don’t know enough of the details and I think probably most of us don’t know. . . . What I can tell you for sure is that Jensen is a remarkable guy who founded and built a remarkable company.”.

Speakers at Semafor’s event approached the subject more gingerly than many in the scrum on X where Huang declared on Tuesday that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Skimming the 58,000 replies to his post, I didn’t see much discussion of the specifics of the case: Huang’s confessing to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia business partner who was allegedly also a spy for China, the questions that raised relating to Nvidia chips possibly being smuggled into China, and reports that he had two additional affairs with Nvidia employees.

#24058. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • According to recent reports, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • In a recent development, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

According to recent reports, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

In a recent development, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an vital role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

It has been revealed that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are right now beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

In a recent development, one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

Sources indicate that in the latest system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Recent findings suggest that many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Sources indicate that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Industry observers note that another crucial benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Upcoming Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

Industry observers note that the research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two notable computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Sources indicate that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments revealed that the upcoming architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

It has been revealed that one of the most significant findings is that the fresh system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Sources indicate that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

According to recent reports, chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Industry observers note that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising upcoming route toward making those machines a reality.

Breaking: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (457 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models.
  • In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.
  • According to recent reports, today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:.

According to recent reports, today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

In a recent development, attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

It has been revealed that all-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Workers are willing to give up higher pay for one thing, new global survey finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Time really is money to many workers.
  • In a recent development, A better salary is no longer the top reason why workers will consider leaving their job in the next year—heck, it didn’t even crack the top three.
  • A better work-life balance topped the reasons why workers might quit their current job, according to a survey of more than 40,000 workers in 36 countries conducted by Adecco, a Zurich-based recruitment and consulting agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Time really is money to many workers. A better salary is no longer the top reason why workers will consider leaving their job in the next year—heck, it didn’t even crack the top three. For the first time since Adecco introduced an annual report on the changing world of work, global workers spanning a wide range of industries are making clear that their time is more valuable. A better work-life balance topped the reasons why workers might quit their current job, according to a survey of more than 40,000 workers in 36 countries conducted by Adecco, a Zurich-based recruitment and consulting agency. But the second and third reasons why workers might switch jobs—seeking out more flexibility and the opportunity to work remotely—also speak to how people are reevaluating how work fits into their lives, and not just the money it provides, according to the report. At a time when workers are increasingly being asked to operate alongside AI agents or even robots, as the report found, they seemingly want to retain some of their humanity. And organizations that don’t want to see a mass exodus of humans should take note, according to Denis Machuel, CEO of Adecco. “We cannot simply ask people to keep pace with technology,” Machuel said in a foreword to the report. “We need to build trust and confidence, to adapt, to give people the freedom to learn and experiment, and protect the flexibility and balance they value.” The survey also highlighted that across seven key indicators, employees generally reported being somewhat less satisfied this year than last. But the biggest decreases were related to flexibility regarding both their working schedule and working location. That’s why the report’s findings also speak to the ongoing tension surrounding stricter return-to-office policies, as Machuel told The Guardian. “Every organization that wants to bring people back to the office struggles with actually implementing these measures to their full extent,” he told the outlet. As for companies with a strict policy of five days per week? “It doesn’t work,” he added. WORKERS WANT AI As artificial intelligence continues to reshape how people work, employers play a key role in how that plays out. The survey found that when AI tools are well integrated into everyday workflows, workers save time for higher-value work—and they feel less overwhelmed by the technology as a result. Nearly three-quarters of workers surveyed use AI agents at work, while 14% work alongside robots, the survey found. These “hybrid workers,” as Adecco dubbed them, report feeling far and away more empowered to shape their work going forward. Compared with their non-hybrid counterparts, these hybrid workers were overwhelmingly more likely to say they’re able to perform at their highest level, that their sense of autonomy over their work has increased in the past year, and that they proactively experiment with different ways of using AI at work. Once again, employers should take note, Machuel says. “When workers help redesign how work gets done, and receive the training and clarity to adapt, AI creates more value, and change becomes easier to navigate,” he said in a statement. “AI delivers its greatest impact when it happens with people and not to people.”.

#24054. Breaking: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1169 w)
