General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Industry observers note that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

In a recent development, by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Sources indicate that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez remarked. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The newly introduced technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Fresh Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

Sources indicate that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez remarked.

Sources indicate that beyond identifying upcoming candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for upcoming medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

According to recent reports, the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

It has been revealed that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he remarked. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

Wall Street’s losses mounted Friday, pulling the S&P 500 10% below its record high set last month, as the sell-off for AI stocks accelerated and the market headed for a sharp weekly loss. The S&P 500 index was down about 2%. If it closes down more than 10% from its October 6 high, it will have entered what professional investors call a “correction.” The benchmark index is on track for a seventh straight day of losses, which would mark the longest such streak since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 3.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which is much less exposed to big technology stocks, fell 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 12:20 p.m. ET. More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the GOP, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 12.4% to $85.16. It is still above its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Chip stocks, big beneficiaries of the buildout of AI data centers, led the decline. Nvidia is falling for the ninth day out of the last 10, down 7.4%. The chipmaker has been under more pressure over worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and cofounder. Advanced Micro Devices dropped 11.7%, and Broadcom fell 11.5%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 9%. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.8%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 3.4%. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93%, from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 0.3% to $91.69 per barrel, despite continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia remarked on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. Markets were lower in Europe and Asia. —By Damian J. Troise and ALex Veiga, AP business writers AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

Wall Street’s losses mounted Friday, pulling the S&P 500 10% below its record high set last month, as the sell-off for AI stocks accelerated and the market headed for a sharp weekly loss.

According to recent reports, the S&P 500 index was down about 2%. If it closes down more than 10% from its October 6 high, it will have entered what professional investors call a “correction.” The benchmark index is on track for a seventh straight day of losses, which would mark the longest such streak since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Sources indicate that the Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 3.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which is much less exposed to significant technology stocks, fell 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 12:20 p.m. ET.

Recent findings suggest that more stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s significant gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their major market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the GOP, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.

It has been revealed that the big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 12.4% to $85.16. It is still above its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

In a recent development, market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Chip stocks, substantial beneficiaries of the buildout of AI data centers, led the decline. Nvidia is falling for the ninth day out of the last 10, down 7.4%. The chipmaker has been under more pressure over worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and cofounder.

It has been revealed that advanced Micro Devices dropped 11.7%, and Broadcom fell 11.5%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 9%.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.8%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 3.4%.

Recent findings suggest that treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93%, from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 0.3% to $91.69 per barrel, despite continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia remarked on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

Markets were lower in Europe and Asia.

—By Damian J. Troise and ALex Veiga, AP business writers.

Latest Update: Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs.
  • Sources indicate that the blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board.
  • Sources indicate that “E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs. The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.

Sources indicate that the blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.

Sources indicate that “E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.

Sources indicate that performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.

Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.

The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.

It has been revealed that the bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.

According to recent reports, also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.

The P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.

The Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.

The Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.

Going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.

As for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.

It has been revealed that there’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

#24049. The one workplace time-suck even artificial intelligence can’t fix

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

The one workplace time-suck even artificial intelligence can’t fix

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI can instantaneously crunch numbers, analyze information, and write emails.
  • Sources indicate that AI can instantaneously crunch numbers, analyze information, and write emails.
  • employees and found that among frequent AI consumers (32% of respondents, who were defined as those who use AI a few times a week or more), 52% spend less time gathering information and 47% spend less time writing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI can instantaneously crunch numbers, analyze information, and write emails. One thing it still can’t do? Save you the time spent in meetings. Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that among frequent AI owners (32% of respondents, who were defined as those who use AI a few times a week or more), 52% spend less time gathering information and 47% spend less time writing. But 83% remarked their time in meetings hasn’t changed, while 78% reported no change in time spent collaborating with coworkers. Although meeting time has dropped from its pandemic-era peak, studies show that meetings still eat up an extraordinary amount of the typical worker’s schedule. A 2024 survey by scheduling platform Reclaim.ai, for example, found that employees spend nearly 15 hours a week in meetings on average—roughly 37% of a standard workweek. The survey’s results suggest that while artificial intelligence is making some tasks more efficient, other aspects of workplace life may be essentially AI-proof. Along with meeting time (and time spent collaborating with coworkers), Gallup also found that 82% of frequent AI users spend about the same amount of time working with customers or clients. And despite AI’s ability to save time on many tasks, even frequent users find their jobs haven’t gotten any easier overall. Nearly two-thirds of frequent AI users (65%) said their roles require about the same mental effort as before, while 21% reported expending less mental effort and 14% claimed their work has become even more demanding. This could be because AI is replacing routine tasks while creating new responsibilities: 21% of frequent users said they now spend more time reviewing and correcting work, and the same percentage reported spending more time learning new skills and tools. However, AI-driven productivity gains have not translated into dramatically higher expectations from employers (or at least not yet). Among employees at organizations that have adopted AI, just 29% told Gallup the technology has raised expectations for how much work they should complete in a day. Frequent AI users are more likely to feel pressure, however: 36% said AI has raised expectations for their output, and 33% said they felt pressure to use the technology to keep up.

Breaking: The hidden human intelligence of design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.” Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility. We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities. DESIGN AND EMOTION Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value. Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user. A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision. Architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions. IMPACT VERSUS HOURS There’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log? I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done rapidly and simply. The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining. It’s important for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact. 6 DESIGN AREAS REQUIRING HUMAN SKILLS Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise: 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties. 2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom. 3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them. 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly. 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they stated understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear. 6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability. When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective. Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

It has been revealed that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Recent findings suggest that whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

In a recent development, wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

According to recent reports, bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and aims auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Recent findings suggest that medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the tech giant claims you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

It has been revealed that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching revision announced last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

According to recent reports, the tabs remain Home, Blueprint, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space.

There’s now a floating action button for the upcoming Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over.

This redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side revision. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the fresh first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

According to recent reports, secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal.
  • Recent findings suggest that videos of the attack revealed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge.
  • With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal. The attack, which led to the partial collapse of the bridge, was significant for a number of reasons. The bridge is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most symbolic assets due to its linking of the occupied Crimean Peninsula and Russia. But perhaps more importantly, the attack's use of Ukrainian connectivity technology highlights the country's lessening of its reliance on Starlink. The modems were crucial to the success of the mission, with the FT reporting that they kept missiles connected to their pilots while they manoeuvred through Russia's air defenses.

Recent findings suggest that videos of the attack revealed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge. Flamingo missiles are capable of traveling at around 590 miles per hour, requiring a stable and reliable video feed. It's reported that the Ukrainians deliberately chose not to use Starshield, the military version of Musk's Starlink, for the operation, with the company's satellite network having been restricted in recent weeks. That restricted service would have been insufficient for the Crimean Bridge attack, forcing Ukrainian forces to find another solution. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted this week that he has not been told why Starlink's connection has been throttled, with neither the White House nor the Pentagon being forthcoming. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, has also so far not provided any explanation. However, relations between Zelenskyy and Musk appear to be strained, with the SpaceX CEO saying that Ukraine had "gone too far" by striking Russian data centers.

With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead. The flying communications towers were used as a relay, boosting the signal sent from individual missiles so that it could more readily reach their pilots. This approach allowed the weapons to fly farther while still maintaining a reliable connection, allowing them to bypass Russian air defense systems and attempts to block their signals in the process. Without the relays, Ukrainian drone pilots have previously had to program missiles with coordinates and then rely on their autopilot system. They were inevitably shot down because they could not be steered away from Russian defenses.

Perhaps ironically, Ukraine isn't the first country to use flying communications towers. Russian forces were using similar technology as early as 2023, before the system began using a Chinese mesh networking system.

Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the latest AI pitch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • Watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • Industry observers note that at Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers. At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in their Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a upcoming Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.” This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that owners didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he said, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.” Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to Max, though it had no input on this column.) AI-optional doesn’t mean AI-free None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027. Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents: The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io. All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies. This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. There’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very crucial to enterprises. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Watching Adobe’s keynote address at the 24th annual annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope it’s walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers.

Industry observers note that at Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in their Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a latest Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.”.

This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that users didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he remarked, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.”.

According to recent reports, instead of a upcoming Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to Max, though it had no input on this column.).

None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy unveiled Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI owners will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027.

In a recent development, adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a fresh level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents: The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io.

It has been revealed that all this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies.

This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a latest kind of customer.

#24041. RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • It has been revealed that usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden. Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it. And RTO might be making things worse. A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface. The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women said they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room. Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks. One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead. Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon. “Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.” As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

#24040. Intel Diamond Rapids reveals signs of life in SC26 demo running live server

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Intel Diamond Rapids reveals signs of life in SC26 demo running live server

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly.
  • The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller.
  • Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its upcoming D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.

The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.

Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has confirmed that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.

It has been revealed that bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it showed off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.

As you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.

In a recent development, based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.

Also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners showed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.

Sources indicate that diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that introduced earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

The future of live entertainment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that change is in the air.
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us. Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater. Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together. Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance. Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for new ways to understand one another. We are entering such a moment now. In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real. For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture. 4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection. 1. The importance of optimism  That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists. That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire. Since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Some platforms make it easy to judge relative friendship, like Snapchat’s publicly viewable “Best Friends” feature. Instagram, however, keeps people’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously remarked the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension. But a new tool from Instagram’s parent company Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse. How Muse can purge your Instagram Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk. One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It rapidly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them. Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted. “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post. Meta’s secret menu Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore. In October, Los Angeles-based social media consultant Rachel Karten noticed a Meta ad on Instagram touting that Muse could let users “see who unfollowed you each week.” “I get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform?” Karten asked in a post sharing a screenshot of the ad. i get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform? pic.twitter.com/SbM6VdcdhV— Rachel Karten (@milkkarten) October 24, 2026 Indeed, Instagram has since taken down the ad, as a Meta representative confirmed to Business Insider. Still, the feature remains active in Muse—as long as users know to ask for it.

According to recent reports, the ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your people discover first: broken layouts, usability challenges that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Sources indicate that even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

It has been revealed that most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:.

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce newly introduced violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

In a recent development, these platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

In a recent development, chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

It has been revealed that pricing: Free initiative with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Industry observers note that trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so strategy coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

It has been revealed that percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited owners and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs rapidly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid looks with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Industry observers note that strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free initiative, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with major cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

BackstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Recent findings suggest that trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

It has been revealed that playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that highlights the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Recent findings suggest that visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a newly introduced framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:.

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change reveals up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:.

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

In a recent development, UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

In a recent development, no. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Recent findings suggest that playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.
